extraction: Native meshes triangulated as fans; normals recomputed; negative-determinant winding corrected. Vessel Bézier curves sampled with 12-sided tubes. Blender modifiers not evaluated; the cortical parcels carry no modifiers in the source scene (only small brainstem nuclei carry Subdivision Surface, midline structures Mirror and the corpus callosum Decimate). That was checked with Blender 5.0.1 on a downloaded Startup.blend whose SHA-256 (9de642d9...) differs from source_sha256; spot checks matched the records to 3e-6 display units (see build.sourceInspection). Derived geometry is rebuilt by tools/build_anatomy.py (see build): window and basal cortical parcels are refined with interpolating PN triangles, which round the facets between the source vertices without moving them and add no anatomical detail. Vertex normals point outward and their length stores baked ambient occlusion (0.3-1; markings and instruments keep unit normals).

limitations: Regional reference anatomy, not a patient model or independently validated operative simulation.
Clinoid removal and bone opening are approximate illustrative spatial masks, not validated osteotomies. ACP is part of sphenoid; no marker object relabeled as tissue.
Combinations are reading configurations, not clinically validated combinations. Intradural source describes wide fissure dissection; selecting No displays an evidence conflict.

Native superficial fascia is retained as atlas context but superseded in the study view by illustrative laminae. The deep and superficial temporal laminae and all three fat pads are original illustrations built as offset surfaces over the native temporalis and skull; their thickness, extent, split height and attachments are illustrative values, not atlas segmentations.
Separated-plane view exaggerates spacing to reveal layer order; it is not an operative tissue position.
Six supplied PDFs reviewed; exact subject-specific 3D geometry cannot be recovered from 2D images.
Song muscle-splitting branch depicts intact atlas muscle and describes its en-bloc exposure; an exact fiber split is not inferred.

Cortex keeps its native atlas positions, except about 15 vertices per side at the bone-window rim moved inward by at most 2.8 mm so they stay under the illustrative dura; brain retraction and cortical deformation are not modeled. Window parcels are smoothed with PN triangles, which remove faceting but keep the coarse atlas gyral form; sulci read as seams between separate parcels. An illustrative backing (native white-matter surface) fills those seams. The orbital gyri, lateral orbital sulcus and temporal pole stay context-only so they do not cover the optico-carotid corridor; some dark gaps remain deep in the corridor.

The Sylvian arachnoid and superficial veins are original illustrations: the arachnoid is a translucent sheet over the atlas cortex, drawn milkier over the fissure, that opens along a schematic fissure line. It is left out over the context-only orbital gyri and temporal pole. Opercular separation, the depth of the split and cisternal arachnoid are not reconstructed.

Venous courses (superficial middle cerebral vein with tributaries, sphenoparietal and cavernous sinuses, superficial temporal vein, Trolard and Labbé veins) are derived from atlas cortex, bone and arteries, not segmented; one typical drainage pattern is shown and calibres are approximate. The cavernous sinus is placed from parasellar landmarks (native oculomotor and abducens nerves), not fitted to the atlas carotid, whose horizontal cavernous segment lies lower than typical; only the upper part of the carotid's ascending genu lies inside it, and the dural layers of its wall are not modeled.

Local dura is a sheet fitted under the native inner table, covering the bone window with a margin and the lateral sphenoid ridge; its extent and single-surface thickness are illustrative. Where the atlas cortex crosses the atlas inner table the sheet runs inside the bone slab within the window; at the window rim it stays under the inner table, so atlas cortex can show through it in a few small spots at the cut edge.

The scalp (skin with subcutaneous tissue, galea/temporoparietal fascia, pericranium) is an original illustration built as offset shells over the atlas skull, temporalis and illustrative temporal layers; thicknesses (about 7 mm in total over the vault), extent and cut lines are illustrative. The incision follows the upper part of the atlas schematic incision marking; its lower part is redrawn to begin on the zygomatic arch about 1 cm in front of the estimated tragus and to pass behind the guide's bone window. Hair, the auricle and the face are not modeled. Where the scalp covers them, the atlas superficial temporal artery and frontal branch and the illustrative superficial temporal vein are moved radially into the subcutaneous layer (their atlas course lies deeper, at the bone / temporal-fascia level); below the zygomatic arch they keep the atlas course. Atlas context sheets that coincide with the scalp (epicranial aponeurosis, frontalis, occipitalis, temporoparietalis, atlas superficial temporal fascia) are hidden while the scalp is drawn.

Soft-tissue motion is schematic: in the renderer the scalp, pericranial, temporal fascial, temporalis and dural flaps peel from their free edge toward a straight illustrative hinge and roll over it, with the hinge height taken from the data; at the end of the fold the reflected scalp, galeal, fascial and pericranial flaps are laid toward the face about 9 mm above the facial skeleton or stationary scalp (a stand-in for the rolled sponge and the facial soft tissue the model lacks), and the dural leaf rests on the bone beyond the window rim. The incision edges part slightly more than in life for visibility, more so while the galea is closed. These are not soft-tissue simulations: the reflected temporalis can touch the rolled scalp near the lateral orbital rim, and hooks, sponges and drapes are not modeled.

Patient positioning turns the whole atlas head rigidly about an estimated craniocervical pivot (between the occipital condyles). The default (about 20 degrees contralateral rotation and 20 degrees extension) follows the example in Rodriguez Rubio et al. and is target-dependent; the neck, body, table tilt and venous-drainage elevation are not modeled, and the head holder, its pin sites, the table edge and the orientation gizmo are schematic drawings, not measured equipment positions.

Schematic markings are drawn as smooth tubes about 0.7 mm in radius at least 0.1 mm above the surface they annotate (skin markings typically 0.1-0.3 mm; outlines projected onto bone and dura ride an envelope typically 0.4-0.6 mm above it, up to about 1.8 mm at dash ends); they mark regions, trajectories and sequences for teaching, not measured landmarks. The prepared-field outline was widened to enclose the illustrative incision marking (at least 8 mm away from the scalp's free edge; at the zygomatic arch it runs along that edge and the incision marking stops 5 mm above it), and stitch, tack-up and fixation marks are evenly spaced or radial by design; galeal stitches are drawn on the galea, skin stitches on the skin. Deep markings are smoothed only and can pass behind vessels or partly into bone.

Ambient occlusion is precomputed per vertex in the rest pose; reflected flaps keep rest-pose shading, and the scalp layers, dura and fascial sheets occlude only themselves. Surgical-palette surface texture is procedural decoration, not anatomy: it draws no dural or pial vessels, and the layered tones of the cut bone edge are estimated in the renderer, not modeled.
Instrument directions illustrate a qualitative surface entry only. They are not exact surgical placements, collision-checked paths, measured angles or patient-specific trajectories.

Right, Left and Both contexts are selectable; Both applies the procedure on the right. Dura, temporal layers, veins, arachnoid, sulcal backing and scalp layers are fitted independently to native left anatomy (the atlas left side is close to a mirror of the right; the left scalp reuses the right side's cut layout); left markings are redrawn by the same code on native left anatomy (the deep Sylvian, clinoid and optico-carotid markings and the instruments mirror the right).

papers.title: Immersive Surgical Anatomy of the Pterional Approach
papers.access: Supplied full PDF reviewed; text available offline; PDF included in bundle
papers.summary: A layered anatomical study with published volumetric models. Describes the pterional exposure, fascial alternatives, basal bone work and dural opening. Useful as the common anatomical reference; its models remain separate from this atlas.

papers.title: Extradural anterior clinoidectomy: Technical nuances from a learner’s perspective
papers.citation: Mishra, Leão & Rosito · Asian J Neurosurg · 2017 · 12:189–193
papers.access: Supplied full PDF reviewed; text available offline; PDF included in bundle
papers.summary: Describes extradural exposure of the anterior clinoid and its relationships to the optic nerve, carotid artery and cavernous sinus. Includes subfascial exposure. The cadaveric technique is a source for this branch, rather than a rule that every pterional exposure needs clinoidectomy.

papers.title: Anterior clinoidectomy: Description of an alternative hybrid method and a review of the current techniques with an emphasis on complication avoidance
papers.citation: Kulwin, Tubbs & Cohen-Gadol · Surg Neurol Int · 2011 · 2:140
papers.access: Supplied full PDF reviewed; text available offline; PDF included in bundle
papers.summary: Distinguishes intradural, extradural and hybrid clinoidectomy. Its intradural description places dural opening and Sylvian dissection before clinoid work. The hybrid method is an additional technique, not a synonym for either selector choice.
papers.section: PDF p.2, Intradural anterior clinoidectomy. Figures on p.4 show hybrid method.

papers.title: Subfascial temporalis dissection preserving the facial nerve in pterional craniotomy—technical note
papers.citation: Horimoto et al. · Neurol Med Chir (Tokyo) · 1992 · 32:36–37
papers.summary: Reports subfascial temporalis dissection and reconstruction, with preservation of the frontotemporal facial nerve branch. The abstract supports the technique name and purpose; detailed maneuvers and figures require the full paper.
papers.section: Abstract only; no detailed procedure inferred

papers.title: The Usefulness of Subfascial Temporalis Dissection Method in Pterional Craniotomy
papers.citation: Song et al. · J Korean Neurosurg Soc · 1997 · 26:235–240
papers.access: Supplied full PDF reviewed; text available offline; PDF included in bundle
papers.summary: A clinical comparison of muscle-splitting, interfascial and subfascial dissections. In its muscle-splitting group, the methods describe reflecting scalp and temporalis together without separating the scalp from temporal fascia. Figure 1 demonstrates subfascial dissection. This is not a specification of a precise intramuscular fiber split.
papers.section: PDF p.2 (printed p.236), Methods; Figure 1 shows subfascial dissection

papers.title: Microsurgical anatomy of the temporal lobe: part 2—sylvian fissure region and its clinical application
papers.access: Supplied full PDF reviewed; text available offline; PDF included in bundle
papers.summary: An extensive anatomical study of the Sylvian region. Figure 11 shows progressive right-sided opening and its opercular and insular compartments; Figure 12 shows left-sided examples. The model is a reference atlas comparison, not a reconstruction of those specimens.
papers.section: PDF p.18, Figure 11A–C: right pterional progressive dissection

papers.title: A Low Subfrontal Dural Opening for Operative Management of Anterior Skull Base Lesions
papers.citation: Cler et al. · J Neurol Surg B Skull Base · 2023 · 84:201–209 (online 2022)
papers.access: Supplied full PDF reviewed; text available offline; PDF included in bundle
papers.summary: Describes a limited low subfrontal opening over the optico-carotid cistern with reduced frontal, temporal and Sylvian exposure. Figure 1 compares it with C- and Y-shaped openings. The model uses a limited smooth illustrative window for this branch; suitability depends on the actual lesion and anatomy.
papers.section: PDF pp.2–3, Figure 1 and Surgical Technique

steps.title: Identify the pterion and target
steps.body: Identify the meeting point of the frontal, parietal, temporal and sphenoid bones and relate it to the planned intracranial target. This establishes the frontotemporal route and the amount of frontal, temporal or basal exposure that will be needed.
steps.note: The illustrative scalp is hidden in this step so the sutures meeting at the pterion stay visible; it covers the region again from positioning onward (Layers & View › Scalp Skin shows it here). On the surface the pterion lies roughly two finger-breadths above the zygomatic arch and a thumb-breadth behind the frontal process of the zygomatic bone, the usual bedside estimate.

evidence.origin: Technique synthesis; preparation and closure also follow the procedural outline supplied for this guide.

steps.title: Position and immobilize the head
steps.body: Position supine with the head elevated for venous drainage and secured in a Mayfield or Sugita head frame. Rotate away from the operative side and tailor extension to the target so gravity can relax the frontal lobe without allowing the orbital roof to obscure the optic–carotid corridor.
steps.note: Rodriguez Rubio et al. describe about 15–20° contralateral rotation and 20° extension in their example, with target-dependent adjustment. The model turns the atlas head rigidly by those default angles about an estimated craniocervical pivot; adjust them under Layers & View › Patient Position. The cyan arrow on the scalp draws in as the head turns and marks the direction of the contralateral rotation (seen best from the top of the head or in Surgeon's View). Neck, body and venous-drainage elevation are not modeled, and the head holder, pin sites and table edge are schematic.
labels: Right scalp of the vault (skin and subcutaneous tissue) — illustration

steps.title: Prepare and mark the incision
steps.body: Clip hair as needed, prepare the skin and mark a curving frontotemporal incision behind the hairline. Infiltrate the marked line with local anesthetic and epinephrine as appropriate to reduce incisional pain and scalp bleeding.
steps.note: Hair clipping, skin preparation and infiltration are described, not modeled; the scalp is an illustrative layered shell.

steps.title: Make the curving scalp incision
steps.body: Begin at the superior border of the zygomatic arch about 1 cm anterior to the tragus and curve toward the midline, preferably behind the hairline. Keep the superficial temporal artery and auriculotemporal region in view while opening the scalp so the flap retains its blood supply.
steps.note: The scalp is an illustrative layered shell (skin with subcutaneous tissue, galea, pericranium) fitted over the atlas skull and temporal layers, not a segmentation. The cut opens along an illustrative course from the zygomatic arch toward the midline: its upper part follows the atlas schematic marking, its lower part is redrawn to start on the arch about 1 cm in front of the estimated tragus. The parting of the edges is exaggerated slightly for visibility.

evidence.section: PDF p.7, Incision of skin; p.8, Figure 3
evidence.origin: Technique synthesis; preparation and closure also follow the procedural outline supplied for this guide.

steps.title: Mobilize the scalp flap
steps.body: Elevate the scalp in the loose tissue plane, exposing pericranium above the superior temporal line and temporal fascia below it. Keep the superficial temporal artery with the flap and protect the temporal facial nerve branches to preserve flap perfusion and forehead movement.
steps.note: The illustrative scalp flap (skin with the galea) is peeled from the incision toward its base, rolled over the orbital margin about a straight hinge and laid toward the face (about 9 mm above the facial skeleton, standing in for the rolled sponge and the facial soft tissue the model lacks); it is not a soft-tissue simulation. The superficial temporal vessels lie in its subcutaneous layer (Full Head Context) and travel with it; facial nerve branches are not shown.
labels: Right scalp flap (skin and subcutaneous tissue) — illustration

steps.title: Develop the subfascial plane
steps.body: Incise both temporal fascial laminae and elevate them together, keeping the interfascial fat within the superficial flap. Separate this fascial envelope from temporalis so the facial nerve branches remain protected in the superficial tissues.
steps.note: Fascial laminae and fat pads are original illustrations. The fascial flap is cut along the scalp incision and peeled forward about the scalp flap's hinge, folding outside the reflected scalp; the posterior temporal fascia stays.

steps.title: Reflect and secure the flap
steps.body: Reflect the mobilized tissues anteriorly over the orbital margin and secure them with scalp hooks or an equivalent retraction system. Distribute tension to keep the bony field accessible while avoiding excessive traction on the superficial tissues.
steps.note: The flap is shown rolled over the orbital margin about a straight illustrative hinge; scalp hooks and sponges are not modeled.

steps.title: Raise pericranium and expose bone
steps.body: Elevate the pericranium and detach the temporalis attachment from the bone as required, preserving tissue for reconstruction. Expose the superior temporal line, frontozygomatic region and temporal squama so burr holes and the bone flap can be planned from visible landmarks.
steps.note: The illustrative pericranium is raised as an anteriorly based flap and folded forward over the reflected scalp; the temporalis anterior to the incision is then peeled from the superior temporal line and reflected inferiorly over the zygomatic arch (its hinge is illustrative). Fish hooks and the musculofascial cuff are not modeled.

steps.title: Place the frontal and temporal burr holes
steps.body: Use the frontozygomatic sutures to locate the MacCarty keyhole region and place a second hole above the zygomatic arch in the temporal squama. Hole number and position are tailored to the required flap and dural adherence; the purpose is to obtain controlled access to the epidural plane before connecting the cuts.
steps.note: Burr holes and drill directions are schematic; millimetric keyhole positioning is not inferred from this atlas.

steps.title: Control bleeding at the burr holes
steps.body: Control bleeding from the exposed bony edges, using bone wax where indicated, and remove loose bony spicules. This clears the entry points and reduces the chance that residual sharp edges will catch the dura.

steps.title: Separate dura from the inner table
steps.body: Use a Penfield dissector to free the periosteal dura from the inner calvarial surface along the intended cuts. Creating this epidural plane protects the dura as the craniotome footplate passes beneath the bone.

steps.title: Raise the frontotemporal bone flap
steps.body: Connect the burr holes with a craniotome and gently elevate the bone flap while completing dural separation. Tailor the frontal and temporal extent to the target so the opening provides the needed line of sight without unnecessary bone removal.
steps.note: The flap follows the illustrative frontotemporal cut and lifts from its inferior edge before moving laterally.

steps.body: Inspect the exposed dura and the margins of the craniotomy for tears and epidural bleeding. Control bleeding before proceeding so the dural surface and basal landmarks remain visible.

steps.title: Flatten the sphenoid wing
steps.body: Reduce the lateral sphenoid wing to lower the basal edge of the frontotemporal corridor. This improves the view along the anterior skull base and reduces the amount of frontal or temporal displacement needed for access.
steps.note: The atlas window summarizes basal bone work; incremental sphenoid drilling is not separately segmented.

steps.title: Extend basal bone removal only if needed
steps.body: If the target requires additional exposure, extend bone removal along the orbital roof, sphenoid ridge or temporal base. These extensions lower or widen the working corridor and are selected for the lesion rather than added routinely.
steps.note: Optional extension is described; its precise osteotomy is not simulated.

steps.title: Place dural tack-up sutures
steps.body: Place dural hitch sutures at suitable craniotomy margins when required and tent the dura toward the bone edge. Apposing the dura to the inner table reduces the epidural space in which postoperative blood can collect.

steps.body: Open the dura in a tailored curving flap and reflect it anteriorly toward the sphenoid base. Protect the underlying cortical vessels and Sylvian veins so the frontal and temporal surfaces can be exposed without injuring the structures beneath the incision.

steps.title: Open the Sylvian arachnoid corridor
steps.body: Identify the superficial Sylvian veins and open the arachnoid interval between the frontal and temporal opercula while preserving veins and arterial branches. Develop the interval toward the insular and basal cisterns, releasing cerebrospinal fluid as appropriate to expose the middle cerebral artery and gain working space with less fixed cortical retraction.
steps.note: The translucent arachnoid and superficial Sylvian veins are original illustrations; the arachnoid opens along a schematic fissure line on native cortex. Opercular separation, small veins and the depth of the split are not reconstructed.

steps.title: Keep the anterior clinoid intact

steps.title: Identify the pterion and target
steps.body: Identify the meeting point of the frontal, parietal, temporal and sphenoid bones and relate it to the planned intracranial target. This establishes the frontotemporal route and the amount of frontal, temporal or basal exposure that will be needed.
steps.note: The illustrative scalp is hidden in this step so the sutures meeting at the pterion stay visible; it covers the region again from positioning onward (Layers & View › Scalp Skin shows it here). steps.title: Position and immobilize the head
steps.body: Position supine with the head elevated for venous drainage and secured in a Mayfield or Sugita head frame. Rotate away from the operative side and tailor extension to the target so gravity can relax the frontal lobe without allowing the orbital roof to obscure the optic–carotid corridor.
steps.note: Rodriguez Rubio et al. describe about 15–20° contralateral rotation and 20° extension in their example, with target-dependent adjustment. The model turns the atlas head rigidly by those default angles about an estimated craniocervical pivot; adjust them under Layers & View › Patient Position. The cyan arrow on the scalp draws in as the head turns and marks the direction of the contralateral rotation (seen best from the top of the head or in Surgeon's View). steps.title: Make the curving scalp incision
steps.body: Begin at the superior border of the zygomatic arch about 1 cm anterior to the tragus and curve toward the midline, preferably behind the hairline. Keep the superficial temporal artery and auriculotemporal region in view while opening the scalp so the flap retains its blood supply.
steps.note: The scalp is an illustrative layered shell (skin with subcutaneous tissue, galea, pericranium) fitted over the atlas skull and temporal layers, not a segmentation. The cut opens along an illustrative course from the zygomatic arch toward the midline: its upper part follows the atlas schematic marking, its lower part is redrawn to start on the arch about 1 cm in front of the estimated tragus. The parting of the edges is exaggerated slightly for visibility.

steps.title: Mobilize the scalp flap
steps.body: Elevate the scalp in the loose tissue plane, exposing pericranium above the superior temporal line and temporal fascia below it. Keep the superficial temporal artery with the flap and protect the temporal facial nerve branches to preserve flap perfusion and forehead movement.
steps.note: The illustrative scalp flap (skin with the galea) is peeled from the incision toward its base, rolled over the orbital margin about a straight hinge and laid toward the face (about 9 mm above the facial skeleton, standing in for the rolled sponge and the facial soft tissue the model lacks); it is not a soft-tissue simulation. The superficial temporal vessels lie in its subcutaneous layer (Full Head Context) and travel with it; facial nerve branches are not shown.

steps.title: Develop the subfascial plane

steps.title: Identify the pterion and target

steps.title: Position and immobilize the head

steps.title: Make the curving scalp incision
steps.body: Begin at the superior border of the zygomatic arch about 1 cm anterior to the tragus and curve toward the midline, preferably behind the hairline. Keep the superficial temporal artery and auriculotemporal region in view while opening the scalp so the flap retains its blood supply.
steps.note: The scalp is an illustrative layered shell (skin with subcutaneous tissue, galea, pericranium) fitted over the atlas skull and temporal layers, not a segmentation. The cut opens along an illustrative course from the zygomatic arch toward the midline: its upper part follows the atlas schematic marking, its lower part is redrawn to start on the arch about 1 cm in front of the estimated tragus. The parting of the edges is exaggerated slightly for visibility.

steps.title: Preserve the myocutaneous layers

steps.title: Mobilize the myocutaneous flap

steps.title: Make the curving scalp incision
steps.body: Begin at the superior border of the zygomatic arch about 1 cm anterior to the tragus and curve toward the midline, preferably behind the hairline. Keep the superficial temporal artery and auriculotemporal region in view while opening the scalp so the flap retains its blood supply.
steps.note: The scalp is an illustrative layered shell (skin with subcutaneous tissue, galea, pericranium) fitted over the atlas skull and temporal layers, not a segmentation. The cut opens along an illustrative course from the zygomatic arch toward the midline: its upper part follows the atlas schematic marking, its lower part is redrawn to start on the arch about 1 cm in front of the estimated tragus. The parting of the edges is exaggerated slightly for visibility.

evidence.origin: Technique synthesis; preparation and closure also follow the procedural outline supplied for this guide.

steps.title: Mobilize the scalp flap
steps.body: Elevate the scalp in the loose tissue plane, exposing pericranium above the superior temporal line and temporal fascia below it. Keep the superficial temporal artery with the flap and protect the temporal facial nerve branches to preserve flap perfusion and forehead movement.
steps.note: The illustrative scalp flap (skin with the galea) is peeled from the incision toward its base, rolled over the orbital margin about a straight hinge and laid toward the face (about 9 mm above the facial skeleton, standing in for the rolled sponge and the facial soft tissue the model lacks); it is not a soft-tissue simulation. The superficial temporal vessels lie in its subcutaneous layer (Full Head Context) and travel with it; facial nerve branches are not shown.

steps.title: Develop the subfascial plane
steps.body: Incise both temporal fascial laminae and elevate them together, keeping the interfascial fat within the superficial flap. Separate this fascial envelope from temporalis so the facial nerve branches remain protected in the superficial tissues.
steps.note: Fascial laminae and fat pads are original illustrations. The fascial flap is cut along the scalp incision and peeled forward about the scalp flap's hinge, folding outside the reflected scalp; the posterior temporal fascia stays.

steps.title: Open the Sylvian arachnoid corridor
steps.body: Identify the superficial Sylvian veins and open the arachnoid interval between the frontal and temporal opercula while preserving veins and arterial branches. Develop the interval toward the insular and basal cisterns, releasing cerebrospinal fluid as appropriate to expose the middle cerebral artery and gain working space with less fixed cortical retraction.
steps.note: The translucent arachnoid and superficial Sylvian veins are original illustrations; the arachnoid opens along a schematic fissure line on native cortex. Opercular separation, small veins and the depth of the split are not reconstructed.

steps.title: Identify the pterion and target
steps.body: Identify the meeting point of the frontal, parietal, temporal and sphenoid bones and relate it to the planned intracranial target. This establishes the frontotemporal route and the amount of frontal, temporal or basal exposure that will be needed.
steps.note: The illustrative scalp is hidden in this step so the sutures meeting at the pterion stay visible; it covers the region again from positioning onward (Layers & View › Scalp Skin shows it here). On the surface the pterion lies roughly two finger-breadths above the zygomatic arch and a thumb-breadth behind the frontal process of the zygomatic bone, the usual bedside estimate.

evidence.origin: Technique synthesis; preparation and closure also follow the procedural outline supplied for this guide.

steps.title: Position and immobilize the head
steps.body: Position supine with the head elevated for venous drainage and secured in a Mayfield or Sugita head frame. Rotate away from the operative side and tailor extension to the target so gravity can relax the frontal lobe without allowing the orbital roof to obscure the optic–carotid corridor.
steps.note: Rodriguez Rubio et al. describe about 15–20° contralateral rotation and 20° extension in their example, with target-dependent adjustment. The model turns the atlas head rigidly by those default angles about an estimated craniocervical pivot; adjust them under Layers & View › Patient Position. The cyan arrow on the scalp draws in as the head turns and marks the direction of the contralateral rotation (seen best from the top of the head or in Surgeon's View). Neck, body and venous-drainage elevation are not modeled, and the head holder, pin sites and table edge are schematic.

The model turns the atlas head rigidly by those default angles about an estimated craniocervical pivot; adjust them under Layers & View › Patient Position. The cyan arrow on the scalp draws in as the head turns and marks the direction of the contralateral rotation (seen best from the top of the head or in Surgeon's View). Neck, body and venous-drainage elevation are not modeled, and the head holder, pin sites and table edge are schematic.

steps.body: Clip hair as needed, prepare the skin and mark a curving frontotemporal incision behind the hairline. Infiltrate the marked line with local anesthetic and epinephrine as appropriate to reduce incisional pain and scalp bleeding.

steps.title: Make the curving scalp incision
steps.body: Begin at the superior border of the zygomatic arch about 1 cm anterior to the tragus and curve toward the midline, preferably behind the hairline. Keep the superficial temporal artery and auriculotemporal region in view while opening the scalp so the flap retains its blood supply.
steps.note: The scalp is an illustrative layered shell (skin with subcutaneous tissue, galea, pericranium) fitted over the atlas skull and temporal layers, not a segmentation. The cut opens along an illustrative course from the zygomatic arch toward the midline: its upper part follows the atlas schematic marking, its lower part is redrawn to start on the arch about 1 cm in front of the estimated tragus. The parting of the edges is exaggerated slightly for visibility.

evidence.origin: Technique synthesis; preparation and closure also follow the procedural outline supplied for this guide.

steps.title: Preserve the myocutaneous layers
steps.body: Preserve continuity between scalp and temporal fascia while defining the edges of the planned myocutaneous flap. Protect the superficial temporal vessels and temporal facial nerve branches so the scalp and muscle can subsequently be mobilized together.
steps.note: No preliminary separate scalp–fascial dissection is included in this branch. The illustrative scalp and galea are hidden in this step so the planned flap margin on the temporal fascia and pericranium stays visible; they stay attached and are reflected together with the temporalis in the next step (Layers & View › Scalp Skin shows them here).

evidence.origin: Technique synthesis; preparation and closure also follow the procedural outline supplied for this guide.

steps.title: Mobilize the myocutaneous flap
steps.body: Mobilize the scalp and temporalis together as a myocutaneous flap while protecting the superficial temporal vessels and temporal facial nerve branches. Keeping these tissues together exposes the pterion without opening a separate scalp–fascial plane.
steps.note: Muscle-splitting terminology is retained from the comparative paper; an exact intramuscular fiber split is not specified or simulated. The illustrative scalp, temporal fascia and temporalis anterior to the incision fold forward together about one hinge; the muscle below the zygomatic arch stays.

steps.title: Reflect and secure the flap
steps.body: Reflect the mobilized tissues anteriorly over the orbital margin and secure them with scalp hooks or an equivalent retraction system. Distribute tension to keep the bony field accessible while avoiding excessive traction on the superficial tissues.
steps.note: The flap is shown rolled over the orbital margin about a straight illustrative hinge; scalp hooks and sponges are not modeled.

steps.title: Raise pericranium and expose bone
steps.body: Elevate the pericranium and detach the temporalis attachment from the bone as required, preserving tissue for reconstruction. Expose the superior temporal line, frontozygomatic region and temporal squama so burr holes and the bone flap can be planned from visible landmarks.
steps.note: The illustrative pericranium is raised as an anteriorly based flap and folded forward over the reflected scalp.

steps.title: Place the frontal and temporal burr holes
steps.body: Use the frontozygomatic sutures to locate the MacCarty keyhole region and place a second hole above the zygomatic arch in the temporal squama. Hole number and position are tailored to the required flap and dural adherence; the purpose is to obtain controlled access to the epidural plane before connecting the cuts.

steps.title: Control bleeding at the burr holes
steps.body: Control bleeding from the exposed bony edges, using bone wax where indicated, and remove loose bony spicules. This clears the entry points and reduces the chance that residual sharp edges will catch the dura.

steps.title: Separate dura from the inner table
steps.body: Use a Penfield dissector to free the periosteal dura from the inner calvarial surface along the intended cuts. Creating this epidural plane protects the dura as the craniotome footplate passes beneath the bone.

steps.title: Raise the frontotemporal bone flap
steps.body: Connect the burr holes with a craniotome and gently elevate the bone flap while completing dural separation. Tailor the frontal and temporal extent to the target so the opening provides the needed line of sight without unnecessary bone removal.
steps.note: The flap follows the illustrative frontotemporal cut and lifts from its inferior edge before moving laterally.

steps.title: Inspect the dura and obtain hemostasis
steps.body: Inspect the exposed dura and the margins of the craniotomy for tears and epidural bleeding. Control bleeding before proceeding so the dural surface and basal landmarks remain visible.

steps.body: Reduce the lateral sphenoid wing to lower the basal edge of the frontotemporal corridor. This improves the view along the anterior skull base and reduces the amount of frontal or temporal displacement needed for access.

steps.title: Extend basal bone removal only if needed
steps.body: If the target requires additional exposure, extend bone removal along the orbital roof, sphenoid ridge or temporal base. These extensions lower or widen the working corridor and are selected for the lesion rather than added routinely.

steps.title: Place dural tack-up sutures
steps.body: Place dural hitch sutures at suitable craniotomy margins when required and tent the dura toward the bone edge. Apposing the dura to the inner table reduces the epidural space in which postoperative blood can collect.
steps.note: Tack-up sutures are described, not modeled.

steps.title: Create the low subfrontal dural opening
steps.body: Make a limited dural opening low over the optico-carotid region, keeping the remaining frontal and temporal surfaces covered. This directs the corridor toward an anterior skull-base target while reducing broad Sylvian exposure.
steps.note: A smooth illustrative window represents the dural opening; reflected sutured leaflets are not reconstructed.

steps.title: Use the limited subfrontal corridor
steps.body: Work through the low subfrontal opening toward the optico-carotid cistern without a routine wide Sylvian split. This concentrates exposure around the skull-base target while preserving the covered frontal and temporal surfaces.

evidence.section: PDF pp.2–3, Figure 1 and Surgical Technique

steps.title: Remove the anterior clinoid intradurally
steps.body: After dural opening, identify the optic nerve, carotid artery and their relationship to the anterior clinoid before removing the required bone under direct intradural observation. Tailor optic-canal unroofing and clinoid removal to the exposure needed while protecting the adjacent neurovascular structures.
steps.note: The conventional description includes Sylvian splitting; the no-split combination retains its evidence note in Papers. Bone removal is approximate.

steps.title: Inspect the target corridor
steps.body: Identify the optic nerve, carotid artery and relevant arterial branches at the end of the selected approach. The lesion-specific treatment proceeds from this exposure; its maneuvers depend on the pathology and are outside this approach sequence.
steps.note: No lesion, aneurysm clipping or tumor resection is simulated.

steps.title: Reapproximate and close the dura
steps.body: After the intradural work and hemostasis, reapproximate the dural margins and obtain a watertight closure, adding a graft if necessary. Restoring this barrier helps contain cerebrospinal fluid and separates the intradural compartment from the wound.
steps.note: Restoration of the illustrative dural surface represents closure; suture lines and grafts are not modeled.

steps.title: Replace and secure the bone flap
steps.body: Return the bone flap to its original position and secure it with suitable plates and screws, adding a central dural hitch if required. Stable fixation restores the cranial contour and protects the underlying dural closure.
steps.note: The flap returns along the reverse path and fixation sites are marked schematically. Any removed clinoid remains removed.

evidence.section: Closure

steps.title: Reattach temporalis and fascia
steps.body: Reapproximate temporalis to its preserved attachment or reconstructive cuff, then restore the fascial layers as appropriate. Re-establishing the muscle position and tissue planes supports mastication and reduces contour deformity.
steps.note: The pericranial flap returns, then the myocutaneous flap (scalp, fascia and temporalis together) folds back into place; muscle sutures are marked schematically.

steps.title: Consider a subgaleal drain
steps.body: If persistent wound oozing suggests a risk of extracranial blood collection, consider a subgaleal drain before the soft tissues are closed. Drain use is conditional on hemostasis and the operative situation rather than an obligatory part of every exposure.

laterality.native: Paired atlas anatomy retains the saved native left and right geometry.
laterality.procedure: Masks act on the selected side; Both operates on the right. The left dura, temporal fascial layers and fat pads, illustrative veins, arachnoid and sulcal backing are built by the same code on native left bone, muscle, cortex and arteries. Left scalp layers are built on native left anatomy with the right side's cut layout mirrored. Left markings are redrawn by the same code on native left anatomy; the deep Sylvian, clinoid and optico-carotid markings and the instruments mirror the right illustrations.

steps.description: Cortical parcels seen through the bone window and along the basal frontal, temporal and Sylvian surfaces are refined with interpolating PN triangles (each triangle -> 4; source vertices unchanged; new surface within about 1 mm of the source facets). Six window parcels per side lose contextOnly. An illustrative sulcal depth backing (native white-matter surface, cropped) closes seams between parcels.

Illustrative dura sheets fitted independently per side between the native inner table and cortex, covering the bone window with a margin and the lateral sphenoid ridge; the sheet enters the bone slab only inside the window cylinder, so it never shows over the cut bone edge.
Illustrative deep and superficial temporal fascial laminae and three fat pads, built as offset surfaces over the native temporalis and skull; left side fitted on native left anatomy.

Illustrative superficial middle cerebral vein system, sphenoparietal and cavernous sinuses, superficial temporal vein and variant Trolard/Labbe anastomotic veins, with courses derived from native cortex, bone and arteries; the cavernous sinus is placed from the native oculomotor and abducens nerves (parasellar landmarks).

Illustrative translucent arachnoid sheet over the window region and Sylvian fissure, with a schematic fissure line used by the renderer to open it; left out over the hidden orbital gyri and temporal pole.

Illustrative scalp over the vault from the brow to the occiput and down to the zygomatic arch: skin and subcutaneous tissue as one closed slab, galea aponeurotica continuous with the temporoparietal fascia, an empty loose areolar gap and pericranium on the outer table (absent over the temporal fascia), built as offset shells over the native skull and temporalis and the illustrative temporal layers. Each side is split into the pterional scalp flap anterior to a curvilinear incision (upper course from the atlas schematic marking, lower course redrawn from the zygomatic arch behind the bone window), an anteriorly based pericranial flap (kept outside the bone window), the stationary operative region and the context-only vault; flap records carry hinge fields for the renderer. The atlas superficial temporal artery and frontal branch and the illustrative superficial temporal vein are re-seated radially into the subcutaneous layer where the scalp covers them.

Schematic markings and instrument arrows redrawn as clean strokes: smooth centrelines resampled evenly by arc length and swept as constant-radius tubes (parallel-transport frames, smooth normals, round caps, cone arrowheads), with at least 0.1 mm of clearance above the surface they annotate (illustrative scalp skin or galea, the bed under the scalp flap, pericranium, bone or dura) enforced against the true mesh; each record's description gives its measured clearance range. Outlines of the renderer's bone window, burr holes and dural openings follow the shader's analytic cuts exactly; the incision and the galeal and skin closure stitches follow the illustrative scalp incision; the prepared-field outline encloses the incision marking; deep markings (Sylvian trace, clinoid, optico-carotid region) are smoothed in place. Left markings are fitted on native left anatomy. Reveal fields are recomputed from the new geometry.

Per-vertex ambient occlusion baked into normal length (range 0.3-1) by voxel ray marching; closed records whose normals pointed inward are flipped outward first. Sheets the renderer moves (dura, fascial layers, fat pads, arachnoid, scalp skin, galea, pericranium) occlude only themselves.
